gloss: A mythical bird that everyone has heard of and no one has seen; a figure for what cannot be grasped.
The first letter of the alphabet, a single straight stroke; a figure for the slender beloved or for a plain line.
The mountain that Farhad carved through for love of Shirin.
The sacred stone set in a corner of the Kaaba at Mecca.
A preface.
A poet's collected poems, usually arranged alphabetically by the last letter of the rhyme.
The mule of Ali.
The Muslim festival that ends Ramadan, a day of celebration.
The stonecutter lover of Shirin, set to cut a channel through a mountain; he killed himself on hearing a false report of her death. Also called the mountain-digger (kohkan).
The archangel who brought revelation to the Prophet.
A lyric poem of rhyming couplets, each couplet complete in itself; the last couplet usually names the poet.
The sacred precinct at Mecca around the Kaaba.
Red dye put on the hands and feet; a bride with fresh henna must sit still until it dries.
A maiden of paradise.
A mythical bird whose shadow falling on a man makes him a king.
A legendary king of Persia who owned a cup in which the whole world could be seen.
A prophet who found the water of life and lives for ever, guiding lost travellers.
1) The Persian king, Farhad's rival for Shirin. 2) Amir Khusrau of Delhi (d. 1325), the great Persian poet, called 'sweet-tongued'.
The beloved of Majnun.
'The madman': Qais, who went mad for love of Laila and wandered the desert.
A legendary painter, proverbial for skill.
Mansur al-Hallaj, the Sufi executed in 922 for crying 'I am the Truth'.
Mir Taqi Mir (d. 1810), the great Urdu poet of Delhi.
The city in Iraq where Ali is buried.
Imam Bakhsh Nasikh (d. 1838), a leading poet of Lucknow.
The real name of Majnun.
A long formal ode, often in praise of a patron or a holy figure.
The direction of prayer, toward the Kaaba; by extension, the object of one's devotion.
'Fragment': a short poem of linked couplets.
A word or phrase repeated at the end of every couplet of a ghazal; also, a section of a divan arranged by the last letter.
An old name for Urdu, especially Urdu poetry.
The angel who keeps the gate of paradise.
A quatrain in a fixed metre.
The angel who brings inspiration.
The princess loved by Farhad and by King Khusrau.
Husain, son of Ali, martyred at Karbala.
The Night of Power in Ramadan, when the Qur'an was first revealed.
A poet's pen name: here Ghalib, and earlier Asad.
A commendation of a book, written as an afterword.
Zuhuri Turshizi (d. 1616), a Persian poet of the Deccan.
Potiphar's wife, who loved Joseph.
The sacred thread worn by Brahmins and, in Persian poetry, by infidels; to tie it is to renounce Islam for love.
